Subject: Performance SLOs & context window follow-up (FinCo)

Hi Alex / Priya 

Thanks again for the time today. Quick recap and a few clarifying questions so our engineering team can size a realistic test and draft a mutual action plan. Short version below, details after.

Summary (from call)
- Target latency: p50 ~<150ms, p95 <350ms for standard 12k token outputs (need confirmation).
- Throughput: baseline ~300 req/s with spikes to 1k req/s during batch ingest windows.
- Concurrency: ~50 concurrent requests expected from the initial service.
- Streaming: you indicated streaming partial outputs is preferred for UX (so users see tokens earlier).
- Context window: core requirement is pulling entire customer transcript + metadata (~4060k tokens) as input; outputs typically 5002k tokens.

Open questions we need to confirm
1) Latency SLOs by output token length: do you expect the same p95 target for 2k+ token outputs?
2) Can you share typical payload sizes (avg input tokens, 95th percentile input tokens, avg output tokens)?
3) Are you ok with a staged SLA where small-context requests have tighter SLOs and large-context requests use relaxed SLOs or dedicated capacity?
4) Any hard constraints on throughput during peak windows (i.e., exact duration and concurrency spikes)?

A few technical notes for context
- Context window size directly affects memory and KV cache behavior. Very large context windows (40k+ tokens) typically increase per-request compute and can increase p95 by 23x depending on model and batching.
- Streaming partial outputs can greatly improve perceived latency for users (they see tokens earlier), but end-to-end completion time still depends on total output tokens.
- We can mitigate tail latencies via dedicated reserved capacity (Redwood Dedicated) and model quantization/variants; we'll propose specific options once we have payload distributions.

Attached: FinCo_SLO_requirements_2026.pdf (your doc from the call)  we’ll reference this in our sizing.

Next steps proposed
- Please reply with the percentile payload sizes (avg, p50, p95 for input and output tokens) and confirm whether the p95 targets you mentioned apply across all output sizes.
- If agreeable, I’d like to schedule a technical deep-dive with Dylan and Dev next week to run through benchmarks and a small pilot.

Thanks 

1) Latency targets: The p95 <350ms target we mentioned was for our short-form assistant flows (<= 512 tokens output). For longer generation tasks (1k2k tokens) we are comfortable with p95 up to ~500ms, but we really want p95 <1s ideally even for larger outputs. The biggest issue for us is tail latency during peak usage windows.

2) Payload sizes: We don’t have exact tokenized counts yet  Priya is working to extract token profiles from our sandbox. Expected roughs: avg input ~6k tokens, p95 input ~45k tokens, avg output ~600 tokens, p95 output ~1.8k tokens. We’ll send a CSV next week with sample payloads.

Hi Alex / team 

Quick technical read based on the numbers above and our initial benchmarks. High-level: the workload is doable, but the context window is the dominant cost driver. Notes below: 

- Context window impact:
  - For autoregressive models, cost scales roughly linearly with input + output length for KV cache ops during generation. Moving from a 8k-token input to 40k tokens commonly increases per-request latency by ~23x on the same model/hardware.
  - Larger context windows also reduce effective batching opportunities because memory per-request is higher; this can increase overall unit cost.

- Model / infra levers:
  - Model variants: smaller/faster models (quantized) can meet tighter p50/p95 for short outputs but may regress on output quality for longer-context summarization tasks. We recommend a hybrid: use a faster variant for short assistant responses, and a larger context-capable variant for long summarization with relaxed SLOs.
  - Streaming: enabling token streaming reduces perceived latency since the client gets the first tokens quickly; however, total completion time is still determined by throughput and model speed for the full token stream. Streaming also reduces tail-time impact on UX.
  - Dedicated capacity: reserving capacity for your peak windows will control tail latencies better than shared hosted capacity; autoscale buffer helps for spikes but can still expose you to higher tails during cold-starts or noisy neighbors.

- Estimations (back-of-envelope on A100-equivalent infra):
  - Short request (<=512 output tokens, input ~6k): p50 ~80120ms, p95 ~220350ms with optimized batching and quantization.
  - Long request (output 1.8k, input ~45k): p50 ~450700ms, p95 ~850ms1.5s depending on batching and whether streaming is used.

- Recommended next steps for pilot:
  1) Provide sample payload CSV (Priya mentioned this)  we’ll run tokenized benchmarks against your 3 corpus types (short assist, medium, long summarization).
  2) Run two benches: hosted (open/shared) and dedicated reserved pool to compare tail latencies and cost.
  3) Validate streaming behavior end-to-end with a small UX client to measure perceived latency.

I’ll spin up a test harness and share results within 48 hours of getting the sample CSV. In the meantime, here’s a link to our internal latency test dashboard for similar workloads: https://redwood.app/tests/finco-llm-latency

Dylan
